clue.text: Clearly public divided by bishop getting attached to repellent fellow

indicators.note: to repel is to drive back, so the word for the fellow is pushed into reverse

parts.note: a don is a university fellow

indicators.note: a word divided by another is split open with the second sitting in its middle

parts.note: a secret that is out is public knowledge
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: A churchman ends up in public alongside some unpleasant fellow, plain for all to see.
explanation.walkthrough: The public piece split by the bishop comes second; the reversed fellow is what it is attached to, so NOD + OU(B)T gives NO DOUBT.
explanation.definitionFit: 'No doubt' is an adverbial phrase meaning certainly or evidently, a synonym of clearly.

clue.text: Wipe pot on the counter at home, grabbing Kleenex to begin with

indicators.note: something that grabs holds another thing within its grip
counter here means running the opposite way, as in anticlockwise

parts.note: a pan is a cooking pot
someone at home is in

indicators.note: what comes to begin with is the first letter

parts.note: first letter of Kleenex

explanation.surface: Cleaning a pot on the kitchen worktop at home, starting with a tissue.
explanation.walkthrough: The kitchen counter is a red herring: 'on the counter' means backwards. NAP + IN then grabs the K.
explanation.definitionFit: A napkin is a cloth or paper square used to wipe the mouth and hands, so a wipe.

clue.text: Hanging very poor designer clothes up

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from the bottom, backwards
as a verb, clothes means covers or wraps, so the words carry the answer inside them

parts.note: the letters running across the end of very, all of poor and the start of designer

explanation.surface: Badly made fashion garments hanging up in a wardrobe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Designer clothes' reads as fashion, but clothes is a verb meaning conceals; the hidden letters are read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Droopy means sagging or hanging down limply.

clue.text: Root, close to victory carried by inferior player?

indicators.note: something carried is held within its bearer

parts.note: an underling is a subordinate, and the question mark flags the loose sense of player

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so its last letter is taken

parts.note: last letter of victory

explanation.surface: A lowly team member, nearing a win, gets carried shoulder-high by the side.
explanation.walkthrough: Root is used adjectivally, as in 'root cause', the cause beneath the obvious.
explanation.definitionFit: A root cause is an underlying cause, so root as a modifier means basic or fundamental.

clue.text: Best part coming up — showing some leg!

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming up means the pieces are read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: A1 means first-rate, written with I standing for the digit 1
a bit is a part

explanation.surface: The cheeky highlight of the show arrives, revealing a flash of leg.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 is a common way of saying top-notch; in crosswords the 1 doubles as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: The tibia is the shinbone, one of the bones making up part of the lower leg.

clue.text: Perhaps ginger daughter seen cuddling student will get married

indicators.note: to cuddle something is to wrap your arms around it, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: ginger is an example of a spice, hence 'perhaps'
L for learner, a student driver
D is the standard abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A red-haired daughter is spotted hugging a fellow student, and wedding bells follow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ginger daughter' reads as a redhead, but ginger is just one example of a spice, and the daughter is a separate piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Spliced is informal British slang for married, from joining two ropes by interweaving their strands.

clue.text: "Cool it, Sir!" blasted highly paid counsellor

indicators.note: something blasted is blown apart, so the letters fly into a new order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An angry client is told to calm down by an expensive legal adviser.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blasted' reads as an angry curse, but it signals the shuffle of the words in quotes.
explanation.definitionFit: A solicitor is a lawyer who advises clients, and counsel is legal advice, so a counsellor in law.

clue.text: Check after voiding punter's first bet

definitions.note: past tense: laid as in 'laid a bet'

indicators.note: after emptying out a letter, the word carries on without it

parts.note: plaid is a checked tartan cloth

indicators.note: first points to the opening letter of the punter

parts.note: first letter of punter

explanation.surface: A gambler double-checks before cancelling a wager.
explanation.walkthrough: Check is a pattern here, not an inspection. Laid is the past of lay, to place a wager.
explanation.definitionFit: To lay a bet is to place one, so laid serves as bet in the past tense.

clue.text: Street noise should be restricted

parts.note: a close is a residential street, often a cul-de-sac
a din is a loud noise

explanation.surface: Residents want the racket on their road curbed.
explanation.walkthrough: In British addresses Close is a common street name, as in Acacia Close.
explanation.definitionFit: Closed in means hemmed in or confined, so restricted in space or movement.

clue.text: Not looking forward to Democrat coming under scrutiny? Quite the opposite

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for Democrat
reading is careful study or scrutiny of a text

explanation.surface: A party member dreads being investigated, though the clue turns the situation around.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry, D under READING would put D last; 'Quite the opposite' puts the scrutiny under the Democrat instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Dreading means fearing something to come, the reverse of looking forward to it.

clue.text: Prominent leader of union interrupting small strike?

indicators.note: something that interrupts breaks into the middle of another thing

parts.note: a prod is a small poke or jab

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter, the one at the head of the line

parts.note: first letter of union

explanation.surface: A trade union head steps into a brief walkout, perhaps with a question mark over its scale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strike' suggests industrial action, but here it is a physical jab; the union's first letter sits inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Proud can mean projecting or standing out from a surface, as a nail head stands proud, so prominent.

clue.text: City's hot food attracting call for extra

parts.note: a balti is a spicy curry cooked in a metal bowl, popular in British curry houses
'More!' is the call for an extra helping or an encore

explanation.surface: A town's fiery dish is so good that diners keep shouting for second helpings.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is', linking the city to its wordplay. A balti is a Birmingham-style curry.
explanation.definitionFit: Baltimore is a large port city in Maryland in the United States.

clue.text: The setter's left a new clue lacking in body and gravity

parts.note: the setter is 'I', so 'the setter is' becomes I'M
port is the left side of a ship
taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new

indicators.note: a word with no body has lost its middle, so only its outermost letters survive

parts.note: the two end letters of clue

explanation.surface: The compiler admits leaving behind a fresh clue that has neither substance nor seriousness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gravity' looks like part of the clue's complaint, but it is the definition, joined to the wordplay by 'and'.
explanation.definitionFit: Gravity in the sense of seriousness or weight of consequence is a synonym of importance.

clue.text: Scrap iron used only at the edges

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

indicators.note: keeping a word only at its edges means retaining just its first and last letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of used

explanation.surface: Scrap iron that has been put to work only around its rim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scrap iron' reads as one phrase, but scrap is the definition, a fight, and iron starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrap is a fight or quarrel, and a feud is a prolonged bitter quarrel.

clue.text: Chic performing live gig around November, it's alluring

parts.note: what is in is fashionable

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so one piece sits inside the other
performing suggests the words are put through their paces and rearranged

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
N is November in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A stylish act playing a concert in the autumn is very appealing.
explanation.walkthrough: Chic is the fashionable sense of 'in'; November is the NATO alphabet code word for N.
explanation.definitionFit: To inveigle is to entice or coax by flattery, so inveigling is luring or alluring.

clue.text: Reportedly soaring mishandling of tin-openers is risk to health

indicators.note: what is reported is heard said, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: soaring means high, which is said the same as the prefix spelt HY-

indicators.note: mishandled items get jumbled up, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Fumbling with kitchen gadgets apparently sends your stress levels sky-high.
explanation.walkthrough: The sound of 'high' supplies only the opening two letters; all ten letters of the openers are then rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Hypertension is high blood pressure, a medical condition that endangers heart and circulation.

clue.text: They delicately cover, say, outbreak of general strikes

parts.note: e.g. means for example

indicators.note: the outbreak of something is its beginning, so the first letter is taken

parts.note: first letter of general
to shell is to bombard

explanation.surface: A general strike is breaking out, which the press handles with care.
explanation.walkthrough: 'General strikes' looks like industrial action; general and strikes are separate pieces, the latter meaning bombards. The definition hints at walking on eggshells.
explanation.definitionFit: Eggshells are fragile casings that enclose eggs, so they form a delicate covering.

clue.text: Work by rogue brought up unforeseen event

parts.note: to act is to work or function
of can mean by, as in 'the works of Dickens'

indicators.note: in a down clue, bringing up means reading from bottom to top

parts.note: a dog is a contemptible scoundrel

explanation.surface: A villain's deeds are dragged up from the past, catching everyone off guard.
explanation.walkthrough: Of in the sense of by appears in phrases like 'a work of genius'.
explanation.definitionFit: An act of God is a natural disaster no one could foresee, a term from insurance and law.

clue.text: Lead-free roof on shed could be grey

indicators.note: free of its lead, a word has lost its leading letter

parts.note: a roof covers a building
a snake casts or sheds its skin

explanation.surface: A garden shed's roof, free of lead sheeting, might look a dull grey.
explanation.walkthrough: Lead suggests the metal used for roofing, but here it is the first letter. Shed is a verb, not the garden hut.
explanation.definitionFit: An overcast sky is clouded over and dull, so grey.

clue.text: Agreement to ignore unlimited bans involved danger for London area

indicators.note: to ignore something is to leave it out, so letters are dropped from the agreement

parts.note: a covenant is a formal agreement

indicators.note: without its limits a word loses its first and last letters, keeping the middle

parts.note: bans with its outer letters removed

indicators.note: involved means tangled or convoluted, so these letters are mixed up

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A deal to overlook boundless prohibitions turns out to be hazardous.
explanation.walkthrough: COVENANT loses the middle of bans; Covent Garden is a district of central London known for its market and opera house.
explanation.definitionFit: Covent Garden is a well-known district in London's West End, so it is an example of a London area.

clue.text: Pro tasted success when making a comeback temporarily

parts.note: pro means in favour of, for

indicators.note: a comeback is a return, so the word goes back the way it came

parts.note: to win is to taste success

explanation.surface: A professional sportsman got a taste of victory on returning, for a while at least.
explanation.walkthrough: Pro looks like a professional player but is the Latin preposition for in favour of.
explanation.definitionFit: For now means for the time being, which is temporarily.

clue.text: Powerful runner finally reined in by Cram

indicators.note: being reined in means being held back within limits, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: to cram is to study intensively

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the word before it

parts.note: last letter of runner

explanation.surface: A strong athlete held back by Steve Cram, the British middle-distance runner.
explanation.walkthrough: Steve Cram is a famous British miler, which makes Cram look like a name; here it is a verb, to revise hard.
explanation.definitionFit: Sturdy means strongly built and robust, a synonym of powerful.

clue.text: Giant howler at Anfield? Reds' second half written off

parts.note: OG is the abbreviation for own goal, a howler in football; Anfield is Liverpool FC's ground

indicators.note: writing off the second half of a word leaves only its first half

parts.note: the first half of reds

explanation.surface: A huge blunder at Liverpool's stadium means the home side's second-half efforts count for nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: Anfield is the home of Liverpool FC, the Reds; the question mark flags the own goal as a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: An ogre is a monstrous man-eating giant of fairy tales.

clue.text: According to commentators, deliberately lost fight, nullifying bookie's tip completely

indicators.note: commentators speak, so the phrase is taken by how it is said

parts.note: a player who threw a fight lost it on purpose

indicators.note: to nullify something is to cancel it, so that letter is struck out

parts.note: a bout is a boxing match

indicators.note: 'tip' keeps only the first letter of 'bookie'

parts.note: first letter of bookie

explanation.surface: Pundits claim a boxer took a dive, wiping out the bookmaker's advice entirely.
explanation.walkthrough: THREW BOUT is said aloud as THROUGH BOUT, and then the bookie's first letter is removed from the fight.
explanation.definitionFit: Throughout means in every part or all the way through, so completely or entirely.

clue.text: Go round park if you want to do this

parts.note: a round shape is O

parts.words: park if you want to do this
parts.note: parked, your speed is zero miles per hour, written 0 MPH

explanation.surface: Driving instructions: circle the block if you are looking for a parking space.
explanation.walkthrough: The second piece is a cryptic definition: to park you must be doing 0 mph, with the zero read as O.
explanation.definitionFit: Go means energy or drive, as in 'full of go', which is what oomph means.

clue.text: Conservative abandons principles to produce works of art

indicators.note: to abandon something is to leave it behind, so that letter goes

parts.note: codes are sets of principles or rules
C is the abbreviation for Conservative

explanation.surface: A Tory politician drops their principles to get things done.
explanation.walkthrough: C is a standard abbreviation for Conservative, the UK party.
explanation.definitionFit: Odes are lyric poems, and a poem is a work of art.

clue.text: Guardiola essentially having big impact after relative sporting success

parts.note: a gran is a grandmother

indicators.note: the essence of a word is at its core, so its central letter is taken

parts.note: the central letter of the nine-letter Guardiola
a slam is a heavy blow

explanation.surface: Pep Guardiola makes his mark after a family member wins a major trophy.
explanation.walkthrough: The heart of Guardiola and the impact come after the relative. Pep Guardiola is the Manchester City football manager.
explanation.definitionFit: A grand slam is winning all the major events in a sport in one season, as in tennis or rugby.

clue.text: Naked adulterers possibly getting intimate

indicators.note: stripped naked, a word loses its outer covering, its first and last letters

parts.note: adulterers are an example of sinners, hence 'possibly'; the middle of sinners is kept

explanation.surface: Unclothed cheating lovers becoming close.
explanation.walkthrough: Adulterers are given as an example of SINNERS, which is then stripped of its first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Intimate can mean private and inward, as one's inner thoughts or innermost feelings.

clue.text: Has an aversion to some in France sheltering tax

indicators.note: to shelter something is to keep it inside, so one word goes within the other

parts.note: des is French for 'some'
to tax is to strain or test

explanation.surface: Someone loathes the way certain French people dodge tax.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tax' reads as a levy but here is a verb, to strain or try.
explanation.definitionFit: To detest is to loathe or hate, which is having a strong aversion to something.

clue.text: Expensive protein product picked up for main course

parts.note: high prices are expensive

indicators.note: to pick up a sound is to hear it, so the words are taken by their sound

parts.note: whey is the protein-rich liquid left from cheesemaking, sold as a supplement

explanation.surface: A pricey protein shake bought for the main meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Main course' wants to be a dinner dish; it is a principal route.
explanation.definitionFit: A highway is a main road, and course in the sense of route or way fits it.
